title: Conditional Quantum Flow Matching for Data-Scarce Physiological Signal Augmentation

paper.title: Conditional Quantum Flow Matching for Data-Scarce Physiological Signal Augmentation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Generative augmentation is a standard remedy for label scarcity in
physiological signal classification, but existing quantum generative
models start from uninformative noise, ignoring class structure that
is already available. We propose Conditional Quantum
Flow Matching (CQFM): a single 306-parameter circuit, conditioned on
both flow time and class label, transports a compact class-conditional
prior toward the target distribution.
Quantum flow matching as published is unconditional, so this is to
our knowledge the first conditional one, and the first EEG
augmentation on a parameterized quantum circuit. A nonnegative
spectral embedding removes the need for tomography at readout. On BCI Competition IV-2a, starting from a prior rather
than noise is worth + 5.1 +5.1 accuracy points over QuDDPM (9/9 subjects),
though at that operating point a class-conditional Gaussian matches
CQFM. Where the prior fails the transport earns its keep: given one
transferred from other subjects it regains + 7.2 +7.2 TSTR points (9/9).

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Deep classifiers for physiological signals such as EEG rarely have enough labels: trials are costly to record, subjects fatigue, and distributions shift across sessions. Generative augmentation is a common remedy, and quantum generative models have recently been applied to it. Quantum GANs synthesize ECG beats [ 11 , 10 ] , parameterized quantum circuits refine latent diffusion for arrhythmia augmentation [ 5 ] , and quantum diffusion models generate financial time series [ 15 ] and images [ 2 ] . All of these start their transport from uninformative noise, the quantum analogue of starting a flow at a standard Gaussian. Quantum machine learning has reached EEG for encoding and representation learning [ 1 , 3 ] , and quantum- inspired GANs have synthesized EEG for privacy [ 9 ] , but not, to our knowledge, an EEG generator on a parameterized quantum circuit. Quantum flow matching (QFM) [ 4 ] extends classical flow matching [ 6 ] to quantum ensembles: a circuit of alternating unitary and partly-measured layers interpolates between two arbitrary density matrices. So far QFM has only been applied to quantum systems themselves, for example Ising thermal states and Jarzynski estimates, and it is unconditional : one trained circuit carries one source ensemble to one target, so generating labelled data would need a separate model per class. Two things are therefore missing for our purpose. The first is a conditioning mechanism. The second is that QFM’s source ensemble does not have to be Haar-random—the freedom that noise-initialized generative models leave unused. In the low-label setting we can build a compact class-conditional prior from the few labeled trials and ask a single conditioned circuit to learn only the remaining transport. Contributions. (i) A conditional QFM model (Sec. 2 ). QFM as published has no conditioning mechanism: one trained circuit carries one ensemble to one target. CQFM folds the flow time and the class label into the same rotation angles, so a single 306-parameter circuit realizes every transport step of every class, trained end-to-end with a differentiable branch-averaged fidelity loss on minibatch-OT-paired interpolants. To our knowledge this is the first conditional quantum flow-matching model, the first applied to classical signals, and the first EEG augmentation method built on a parameterized quantum circuit. An ablation locates the gain in the conditional orthogonal parameterization rather than in the quantum channel. (ii) Encoding design (Sec. 2.1 ). A real-orthogonal ansatz is paired with a nonnegative spectral-magnitude amplitude embedding and class-discriminative bin selection, so generated states can be read out without tomography. (iii) Experiments (Sec. 3 ). Comparisons against the official QuDDPM [ 16 ] , a prior-swap ablation, and tuned classical generators show that the informative prior, not circuit depth, determines generation quality, and that the results hold down to 1024 measurement shots.

sections.heading: 2.1 Spectral encoding
sections.text: Let a labeled trial be X ∈ ℝ C × T s X\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times T_{s}} with label y y . We fit, on the N N -shot labeled subset only : (i) CSP spatial filters [ 12 ] W ∈ ℝ 4 × C W\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times C} (csp-space projection); (ii) per-component masks selecting the K = 16 K{=}16 rFFT bins with the highest ANOVA F F -score of spectral magnitude against the class label. The encoding is the concatenated magnitude spectrum v = [ | F 1 | m 1 , … , | F 4 | m 4 ] ∈ ℝ ≥ 0 64 v=[\,|F_{1}|_{m_{1}},\dots,|F_{4}|_{m_{4}}\,]\in\mathbb{R}^{64}_{\geq 0} , ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -normalized and prepared as an amplitude-encoded state | ψ ⁡ ( v ) ⟩ = ∑ j v j ​ | j ⟩ |\psi(v)\rangle=\sum_{j}v_{j}|j\rangle on n = 6 n{=}6 qubits. This is feature-space augmentation: the magnitude encoding cannot be inverted back to raw EEG, and all downstream evaluation takes place in the same space. Two design choices matter. Complex spectra did not learn at all (0.258 across nine subjects, against 0.25 chance); discarding phase reaches 0.389, so single-trial spectral phase is mostly noise here. And keeping amplitudes near-nonnegative removes the need for tomography at readout. The real-orthogonal transport does not preserve nonnegativity exactly, but because it starts near identity from nonnegative inputs, the negative-amplitude probability mass stays below 0.2 % 0.2\% in our measurements, and the v j = p j v_{j}=\sqrt{p_{j}} computational-basis readout removes the remainder.

sections.heading: 2.2 Class-conditional prior
sections.text: For each class c c we fit a diagonal Gaussian 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ c , σ c 2 ) \mathcal{N}(\mu_{c},\sigma_{c}^{2}) to the encoded subset vectors and take the normalized samples as the prior ensemble ρ prior c \rho^{c}_{\mathrm{prior}} . This is the informative source that QFM allows and that noise-initialized models do not use.

sections.heading: 2.3 The CQFM model
sections.text: QFM [ 4 ] provides the transport primitive: circuits with measured ancillas can interpolate between arbitrary ensembles. The conditioning mechanism, training objective, prior construction, and encoding design described here are new. Each flow step is a channel rather than a unitary. The system state and one ancilla pass through L L layers of R y R_{y} rotations and ring- C ​ R y CR_{y} entanglers (a real-orthogonal family, so states remain real, and the map is close to the identity at small angles); the ancilla is then measured, and an R y R_{y} correction conditioned on the outcome is applied to the system. The rotation angles are θ l , q + w l , q ​ t + e c , l , q \theta_{l,q}+w_{l,q}\,t+e_{c,l,q} , so the flow time t t and class label c c enter a single shared circuit: 306 parameters in total, namely 42 base angles θ \theta , 42 time weights w w , 168 class embeddings e e (4 classes), 42 entangler angles, and 12 outcome-conditioned corrections. A fixed CNOT ring was tried and discarded: it is a basis permutation and destroys the near-identity initialization small-step flows need. The measured ancilla, by contrast, turns out not to be load-bearing (Sec. 3 ). Training samples a class c c , a prior point x 0 x_{0} , a data point x 1 x_{1} , and a step k k ; the circuit at t = k / T t=k/T is trained to map the normalized interpolant x t ∝ ( 1 − t ) ​ x 0 + t ​ x 1 x_{t}\propto(1{-}t)x_{0}+tx_{1} to x t + 1 / T x_{t+1/T} . This is a discrete-time analogue of conditional flow matching [ 6 ] : a per-step map regression along OT-paired interpolant paths, without the marginal guarantees of a continuous vector field, so distributional quality is checked empirically in Sec. 3 . The loss is the branch-averaged infidelity ∑ r p r ​ ( 1 − ⟨ ψ r | ψ tgt ⟩ 2 ) \sum_{r}p_{r}\,(1-\langle\psi_{r}|\psi_{\mathrm{tgt}}\rangle^{2}) , which can be differentiated without sampling; at generation time the ancilla outcomes are sampled. Pairs ( x 0 , x 1 ) (x_{0},x_{1}) are matched by minibatch optimal transport [ 14 ] , which reduced the loss floor from 0.025 to 0.0175. We use T = 10 T{=}10 steps, L = 6 L{=}6 layers, and 1500 Adam steps.

sections.heading: 3 Experiments
sections.text: Setup. BCI Competition IV-2a [ 13 ] (9 subjects, 4-class motor imagery, 22 channels): session T for training, session E held out. Low-label protocol: N ∈ { 10 , 25 , 50 , 72 } N\in\{10,25,50,72\} labeled trials per class, 5 subsampling seeds; the encoder, priors, generative models, and classifiers see only the N N -shot subset. Baselines: no augmentation; the informative prior alone (no transport); CQFM with a Haar prior (prior-swap ablation, identical circuit and budget); the official QuDDPM implementation [ 16 ] (per-class models, T = 10 T{=}10 , L = 6 L{=}6 , 3360 parameters total vs. CQFM’s 306; Fig. 1 c); and classical conditional generators in the identical feature space : a class-conditional Ledoit-Wolf Gaussian, a conditional VAE, and classical conditional flow matching [ 6 , 14 ] with an MLP velocity field at two budgets (332 and 33k parameters), trained with the same prior, OT pairing, steps, and 10-step Euler sampling. Integer hidden widths cannot hit 306 exactly (width 1 gives 198, width 2 gives 332), so the α \alpha study below brackets CQFM from both sides. Metrics: augmented downstream accuracy of an MLP (real N N + 800 synthetic), C2ST [ 7 ] real-vs-generated discriminability (logistic-regression 5-fold CV; 0.5 = indistinguishable), and class-mean log-spectral distance (LSD, dB). Statistics: paired Wilcoxon with subjects as the unit ( n = 9 n{=}9 , seed- and budget-averaged; per-configuration analyses agree in direction). Circuits are simulated exactly (PennyLane 0.38 statevector, PyTorch autograd, CPU); seeds 0 0 – 4 4 are shared across methods. Code, configurations, and all summary results are at https://github.com/ChiShengChen/cqfm-icassp2027 . (b) Fidelity does not change with circuit depth ( N = 25 N{=}25 , 9 subjects × \times 3 seeds). Augmentation helps, and the prior decides by how much (Table 1 , Fig. 2 a). CQFM improves over no augmentation by + 2.5 +2.5 points on average, on 9/9 subjects ( p = .004 p{=}.004 , the floor for n = 9 n{=}9 ), and the improvement holds at every N N . The gap to noise initialization is large: + 5.1 +5.1 points over the official QuDDPM and + 5.4 +5.4 over the Haar-prior ablation (each 9/9, p = .004 p{=}.004 ). The ablation isolates the prior as the cause, since circuit, budget, and training are identical. Fidelity metrics show the same picture (Table 1 , right): noise-initialized transport remains almost perfectly distinguishable from real data (C2ST ≈ \approx 0.98), while informative-prior CQFM reaches 0.80 (9/9 subjects, p = .004 p{=}.004 ); Fig. 3 shows the same contrast directly in sample space. Conditional generators that start from the informative prior, whether quantum or classical, all perform similarly at the operating point. Figure 3: What the models generate ( N = 25 N{=}25 , subject S9—the median subject by CQFM accuracy—seed 0). Top: class-mean spectra, where four separated curves mean class structure is reproduced. Bottom: 15 generated samples of class 1 (colour) over 15 real ones (grey). Every informative-prior model reproduces the CSP envelope and its class structure; noise-initialized QuDDPM produces flat spectra. Depth does not compensate for the prior (Fig. 2 b). Sweeping L ∈ { 2 , 4 , 6 , 8 } L\in\{2,4,6,8\} (9 subjects, N = 25 N{=}25 , 3 seeds) leaves every method’s C2ST and LSD flat, and a 2-layer CQFM still dominates an 8-layer QuDDPM (C2ST − 0.179 -0.179 , 9/9 subjects, p = .004 p{=}.004 ) at 17 × 17\times lower training cost (57 s vs. 981 s). Generation quality depends on where the transport starts rather than on circuit capacity. Finite shots. Reading amplitudes from computational-basis samples at N = 25 N{=}25 , 1024 shots are indistinguishable from exact (.411 vs. .412); 256 shots cost 0.9 points, 5% readout depolarization 0.7. Figure 4: (a) Prior-quality sensitivity ( N = 25 N{=}25 ): as class information leaves the prior, the prior alone drops to chance TSTR while CQFM recovers it through its conditioning. (b) Tuned classical FM at α = 1 \alpha{=}1 (best of four settings per budget). CQFM’s 306 parameters fall between the 198- and 332-parameter models (shaded) and beat both; classical catches up at about twice the size. Does the transport add value beyond its prior? (Fig. 4 ). At the operating point it does not: the prior alone already matches CQFM (Table 1 ). We degrade it with a class-information shrinkage parameter α \alpha ( μ c ​ ( α ) = ( 1 − α ) ​ μ c + α ​ μ \mu_{c}(\alpha)=(1{-}\alpha)\mu_{c}+\alpha\mu , likewise σ c \sigma_{c} ); at α = 1 \alpha{=}1 the prior carries no label information, so any class structure must come from the generator. Every conditional model starts from that same prior, and the classical field is swept over eight sizes (198–33k) with the best of four settings each (Fig. 4 b). Prior-only generation drops to chance TSTR (.241); CQFM recovers .346, beating tuned classical FM at both budgets bracketing its 306 parameters, .261 at 198 ( + 8.5 +8.5 , 9/9, p = .004 p{=}.004 ) and .293 at 332 ( + 5.3 +5.3 , 8/9, p = .008 p{=}.008 ). Classical FM catches up at about twice the size (.355 at 600) and plateaus at .37–.38, above CQFM’s .346 but significant at only one of eight budgets ( p = .04 p{=}.04 ), none after correction. Transferred priors: the misspecified case in practice. The α \alpha knob is synthetic; in practice a misspecified prior comes from other subjects. Pushing their trials through the target’s encoder and fitting the class Gaussian there displaces the prior by 1.3 × 1.3\times the target’s between-class distance on average. Alone it drops TSTR from .411 to .299; CQFM recovers .370 ( + 7.2 +7.2 points, 9/9, p = .004 p{=}.004 ), landing within 1.1 1.1 accuracy points of the target’s own prior ( p = .098 p{=}.098 , n.s.). Against the size-matched classical field CQFM gains + 3.5 +3.5 accuracy and + 4.4 +4.4 TSTR points (9/9 and 8/9, p ≤ .008 p{\leq}.008 ) but loses on distribution match (C2ST + 0.090 +0.090 , LSD + 0.57 +0.57 , both p ≤ .008 p{\leq}.008 ). Class geometry explains both: scaled by within-class spread, class separation is 2.95 in real data, 1.37 in the transferred prior, 1.62 after classical FM and 2.22 after CQFM (9/9 subjects, p = .004 p{=}.004 ). The classical field polishes marginal appearance and leaves the classes nearly as collapsed as it found them. What the quantum channel contributes: nothing measurable. CQFM’s advantage over an MLP velocity field could come from the measured-ancilla channel or from its orthogonal near-identity parameterization. We delete the ancilla and its measurement, changing nothing else: a class-conditional orthogonal flow, 252 parameters at L = 6 L{=}6 and 336 at L = 8 L{=}8 , bracketing CQFM’s 306. It matches CQFM on all four metrics in both regimes and at both depths: TSTR .338 and .343 against .346 at α = 1 \alpha{=}1 , and .369 against .370 with a transferred prior, every comparison within noise (4–6 of 9 subjects, p ≥ .13 p{\geq}.13 ). The measurement layer therefore buys nothing here. What does pay is the parameterization: the same ablated flow, with fewer parameters than CQFM, still beats the tuned MLP field by + 7.7 +7.7 TSTR points at 198 (9/9, p = .004 p{=}.004 ) and + 4.5 +4.5 at 332 (7/9, p = .020 p{=}.020 ). The gain is an inductive bias that happens to be expressible as a quantum circuit, not an effect of measurement.

sections.heading: 4 Limitations and outlook
sections.text: At 6 + 1 6{+}1 qubits the model can be simulated classically: each step is a stochastic mixture of two 64 × 64 64\times 64 orthogonal maps. We therefore claim no quantum computational advantage; the contribution is the model design and the parameter-efficiency evidence above. Results are simulation-based: training uses exact branch probabilities, and the noise analysis covers shots and readout depolarization but not gate-level noise, while barren plateaus at larger scale [ 8 ] remain open. Accuracies live in the 64-dim feature space, well below raw-signal pipelines, and we evaluate one EEG benchmark. Extending to ECG [ 11 , 10 , 5 ] and to raw-signal generation are natural next steps.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: CQFM adds class conditioning to quantum flow matching and uses its main freedom, the free choice of source ensemble: one shared circuit, conditioned on flow time and class, transports a class-conditional prior instead of noise. On BCI IV-2a it beats noise-initialized quantum diffusion by a uniformly significant margin at a fraction of the depth, and survives a prior transferred from other subjects. What carries that is the conditional orthogonal parameterization: ablating the measured ancilla costs nothing measurable.

sections.heading: 6 Compliance with ethical standards
sections.text: This study uses only the publicly available, fully anonymized BCI Competition IV-2a dataset [ 13 ] ; no new data involving human or animal subjects were collected by the authors.

This is feature-space augmentation: the magnitude encoding cannot be inverted back to raw EEG, and all downstream evaluation takes place in the same space. Two design choices matter. Complex spectra did not learn at all (0.258 across nine subjects, against 0.25 chance); discarding phase reaches 0.389, so single-trial spectral phase is mostly noise here. And keeping amplitudes near-nonnegative removes the need for tomography at readout. The real-orthogonal transport does not preserve nonnegativity exactly, but because it starts near identity from nonnegative inputs, the negative-amplitude probability mass stays below 0.2 % 0.2\% in our measurements, and the v j = p j v_{j}=\sqrt{p_{j}} computational-basis readout removes the remainder. 2.2 Class-conditional prior For each class c c we fit a diagonal Gaussian 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ c , σ c 2 ) \mathcal{N}(\mu_{c},\sigma_{c}^{2}) to the encoded subset vectors and take the normalized samples as the prior ensemble ρ prior c \rho^{c}_{\mathrm{prior}} . This is the informative source that QFM allows and that noise-initialized models do not use. 2.3 The CQFM model QFM [ 4 ] provides the transport primitive: circuits with measured ancillas can interpolate between arbitrary ensembles. The conditioning mechanism, training objective, prior construction, and encoding design described here are new. Each flow step is a channel rather than a unitary. The system state and one ancilla pass through L L layers of R y R_{y} rotations and ring- C ​ R y CR_{y} entanglers (a real-orthogonal family, so states remain real, and the map is close to the identity at small angles); the ancilla is then measured, and an R y R_{y} correction conditioned on the outcome is applied to the system. The rotation angles are θ l , q + w l , q ​ t + e c , l , q \theta_{l,q}+w_{l,q}\,t+e_{c,l,q} , so the flow time t t and class label c c enter a single shared circuit: 306 parameters in total, namely 42 base angles θ \theta , 42 time weights w w , 168 class embeddings e e (4 classes), 42 entangler angles, and 12 outcome-conditioned corrections. A fixed CNOT ring was tried and discarded: it is a basis permutation and destroys the near-identity initialization small-step flows need. The measured ancilla, by contrast, turns out not to be load-bearing (Sec. 3 ). Training samples a class c c , a prior point x 0 x_{0} , a data point x 1 x_{1} , and a step k k ; the circuit at t = k / T t=k/T is trained to map the normalized interpolant x t ∝ ( 1 − t ) ​ x 0 + t ​ x 1 x_{t}\propto(1{-}t)x_{0}+tx_{1} to x t + 1 / T x_{t+1/T} . This is a discrete-time analogue of conditional flow matching [ 6 ] : a per-step map regression along OT-paired interpolant paths, without the marginal guarantees of a continuous vector field, so distributional quality is checked empirically in Sec. 3 . The classical field polishes marginal appearance and leaves the classes nearly as collapsed as it found them. What the quantum channel contributes: nothing measurable. CQFM’s advantage over an MLP velocity field could come from the measured-ancilla channel or from its orthogonal near-identity parameterization. We delete the ancilla and its measurement, changing nothing else: a class-conditional orthogonal flow, 252 parameters at L = 6 L{=}6 and 336 at L = 8 L{=}8 , bracketing CQFM’s 306. It matches CQFM on all four metrics in both regimes and at both depths: TSTR .338 and .343 against .346 at α = 1 \alpha{=}1 , and .369 against .370 with a transferred prior, every comparison within noise (4–6 of 9 subjects, p ≥ .13 p{\geq}.13 ). The measurement layer therefore buys nothing here. What does pay is the parameterization: the same ablated flow, with fewer parameters than CQFM, still beats the tuned MLP field by + 7.7 +7.7 TSTR points at 198 (9/9, p = .004 p{=}.004 ) and + 4.5 +4.5 at 332 (7/9, p = .020 p{=}.020 ). The gain is an inductive bias that happens to be expressible as a quantum circuit, not an effect of measurement. 4 Limitations and outlook At 6 + 1 6{+}1 qubits the model can be simulated classically: each step is a stochastic mixture of two 64 × 64 64\times 64 orthogonal maps. We therefore claim no quantum computational advantage; the contribution is the model design and the parameter-efficiency evidence above. Results are simulation-based: training uses exact branch probabilities, and the noise analysis covers shots and readout depolarization but not gate-level noise, while barren plateaus at larger scale [ 8 ] remain open. Accuracies live in the 64-dim feature space, well below raw-signal pipelines, and we evaluate one EEG benchmark. Extending to ECG [ 11 , 10 , 5 ] and to raw-signal generation are natural next steps. 5 Conclusion CQFM adds class conditioning to quantum flow matching and uses its main freedom, the free choice of source ensemble: one shared circuit, conditioned on flow time and class, transports a class-conditional prior instead of noise. On BCI IV-2a it beats noise-initialized quantum diffusion by a uniformly significant margin at a fraction of the depth, and survives a prior transferred from other subjects. What carries that is the conditional orthogonal parameterization: ablating the measured ancilla costs nothing measurable. 6 Compliance with ethical standards This study uses only the publicly available, fully anonymized BCI Competition IV-2a dataset [ 13 ] ; no new data involving human or animal subjects were collected by the authors.
